In this video, you'll learn what Skills are, how they work under the hood, and how to build your own, step by step.
So, what exactly is a Skill?
A Skill is simply a folder. It holds instructions, scripts, and resources that Claude can discover and load whenever a task needs them.
Every Skill is built around one required file, called SKILL dot M D.
Alongside it, you can add optional extras — like Python scripts, document templates, or reference notes.
Think of it as packaged know-how: the 'how we do it here' for a specific task. And the best part? Claude picks the right Skill automatically. You don't have to ask for it.
Let's open a SKILL dot M D file, and look inside.
At the top is the frontmatter — a short block of YAML between two lines of dashes. It holds two fields: a name, and a description.
The description is the most important line in the whole Skill. It tells Claude what the Skill does, and exactly when to use it.
Below the frontmatter come the instructions, written in plain Markdown — steps, rules, and examples, just like you'd explain them to a new teammate.
Finally, the Skill can point to other files — such as a script to check your work, or a template to start from. Claude opens them only when it needs them.
Now, here's the secret that makes Skills so efficient: progressive disclosure.
Level one is the metadata — just the name and the description. It's always loaded, and costs only about a hundred tokens per Skill.
Level two is the body of SKILL dot M D. Claude reads it only when your request matches the Skill's description.
Level three is everything else — the bundled files and scripts. Claude opens or runs them only if the task actually requires it.
This means you can install many Skills at once, and Claude still loads only what each task truly needs.
So what happens when you actually use a Skill? Let's follow a request.
Step one: you ask for something in plain language — for example, create a quarterly report for my team.
Step two: Claude scans the descriptions of all your installed Skills.
Step three: it finds a match, and loads that Skill's instructions.
Step four: it follows the steps, and runs any scripts the Skill includes.
And step five: you get a polished result that follows your rules — consistently, every single time.
Why are Skills such a big deal? There are four key reasons.
First, they're composable. Skills stack together, and Claude can combine several of them for a single task.
Second, they're portable. The same Skill format works across the Claude apps, Claude Code, and the API.
Third, they're efficient. Only what's needed gets loaded, so your context stays light and fast.
And fourth, they're powerful. Skills can include real code, for results that are exact and reliable.
Anthropic provides ready-made Skills, and you can also create your own.
The Excel Skill builds real spreadsheets, with formulas, formatting, and charts.
The Word Skill creates and edits documents, with styles, tables, and tracked changes.
The PowerPoint Skill turns your content into polished slide decks.
The PDF Skill can create PDFs, fill in forms, extract text, and merge or split files.
The Skill Creator is a helper Skill. Just chat with Claude, and it designs and packages a new Skill with you.
And of course, there are your own custom Skills — your brand rules, your team's processes, and your templates.
One of the best things about Skills: you build them once, and use them everywhere.
In the Claude apps, simply turn on Skills in Settings, under Capabilities.
In Claude Code, place your Skills in the dot claude, slash skills folder, or install them through plugins.
Developers can also add Skills to their own agents, using the Claude API and the Agent SDK.
And on Team and Enterprise plans, admins can share Skills with the entire organization.
You might be wondering how Skills compare to other Claude features.
Skills answer the question: how do I do this? They load on demand, and they're perfect for repeatable workflows.
Projects answer: what should I know? They keep background files and context available inside a project.
MCP answers: what can I reach? It connects Claude, live, to external apps and data.
And prompts are for just this once — instructions for a single conversation.
They work best together. MCP gives Claude access, and Skills teach it the procedure.
Ready to create your own Skill? It takes just four steps.
First, pick a workflow you repeat often. Or simply ask the Skill Creator to help you.
Second, write your SKILL dot M D: a name, a clear description, and then the instructions.
Third, add any scripts or templates. Then zip the folder and upload it in the Claude app, or drop it into your skills folder in Claude Code.
And fourth, test it with real tasks, and sharpen the description until Claude uses it at exactly the right moments.
So, what kinds of Skills could you build today? Here are some ideas.
Brand guidelines that keep every document on brand. Report templates with the same structure every time. And data analysis that follows your team's exact method.
Code review checklists. Financial models with consistent logic. And meeting notes with clear summaries and action items.
Onboarding guides for new team members. Or research papers with proper academic structure and citations. If you do it more than once, it can be a Skill.
Before we wrap up, here are six best practices for great Skills.
One: write a precise description. Say what the Skill does, and when to use it.
Two: keep each Skill focused on one job. You can always combine several.
Three: show examples of great output, so Claude knows exactly what good looks like.
Four: use scripts for steps that must be exact and repeatable.
Five: only install Skills from sources you trust, because Skills can run code.
And six: test and iterate. Refine your Skills with real tasks over time.
Let's recap in one line: package, load, reuse.
Claude Skills turn your expertise into reusable know-how, that Claude loads exactly when it's needed.
